Base R and the tidyverse inside sasonr

Source: vignettes/articles/dev-base-vs-tidyverse.Rmd
dev-base-vs-tidyverse.Rmd

This note records which parts of sasonr are written in base R and which parts use the tidyverse, why the split falls where it does, and which questions are still open. It is a design note, not a user guide.

Layering

Layer Language Evidence (calls in R/)
Value runtime: functions, formats, rounding base R + stats:: functions.R: 0 tidyverse, 66 base; stats:: 97 across the package
Exact statistics (moments, CSS) base R, bit-level stats_exact.R: 0 tidyverse
PROC engines (MEANS, FREQ, …) base R for the arithmetic, tibble only at the result boundary proc_means.R: 84 base / 2 tidyverse; proc_freq.R: 172 base / 8 tidyverse
DATA step execution two code generators: a vectorised path emits dplyr pipelines, the row-wise path emits base R codegen_tidy.R: 16 dplyr/tibble calls
PROC SQL own parser and R evaluation; DuckDB is a candidate executor for joins/aggregations, never a passthrough sql_exec.R: DBI/duckdb 4 each
Translation output (sas_translate()) planned: an idiomatic mode that emits tidyverse code and a faithful mode that emits sas_rt_* calls not implemented yet

What the tidyverse is used for, and why those uses are safe

These are structural, not numeric, operations, where dplyr’s semantics are either exact or do not affect the results:

  • dplyr::if_else() for conditional assignment in vectorised code — stricter than ifelse(), which drops attributes;
  • dplyr::lag() for LAG, whose semantics is exactly “previous row”;
  • dplyr::coalesce() for COALESCEC — first non-missing argument;
  • dplyr::bind_rows() and tibble::as_tibble() for SET, OUT= data sets and the result container.

Why the value layer cannot use the tidyverse

lubridate: a different calendar

sasonr’s calendar does not treat years divisible by 4000 as leap years. The runtime implements that calendar explicitly (runtime.R, skip4000_g/sas_day_to_greg), while lubridate follows the proleptic Gregorian calendar, so dates beyond 4000 differ. Beyond that: SAS dates are days and datetimes are seconds since 1960-01-01, Date/POSIXct add a timezone and a second conversion layer, the valid range is 1582-01-01..20000-12-31, and the SAS informats parse with their own rules (MDY-before-DMY preference, YEARCUTOFF, invalid input sets _ERROR_ and returns missing). None of that maps onto lubridate’s parsers.

stringr: fixed width, bytes and missing values

SAS character values are fixed-length and blank padded, a missing character is a blank string (not NA), and LENGTH/SUBSTR/$w. widths count bytes in the session encoding. stringr returns variable-length strings, propagates NA, counts Unicode code points and delegates case mapping to ICU/locale. Base substr/toupper is not perfect either, but its behaviour is deterministic and can be pinned to the SAS rules.

dplyr aggregations and ordering

The moments must be accumulated in observation order with plain double arithmetic: R’s sum() accumulates in long double and differs in the last bits, which is why the CSS formula is written out by hand (stats_exact.R). dplyr::summarise() would reintroduce sum(). arrange() places NA last, while missing values sort first in SAS, and group_by() does not promise SAS’s group order. The PROC listings also need control over the column layout to the character, which a summarise() result does not give.

tidyr

PROC output is a fixed-width text listing; reshaping only changes the data frame shape, while the order, names and labels still have to be produced exactly. Adding tidyr would buy little and cost a dependency.

Where tidyverse is fine

  • The planned idiomatic output of sas_translate(): readable dplyr code for people who keep the translation. It does not decide the results; the numerical results still come from sas_f_*/sas_put()/sas_input().
  • User-facing examples and vignettes.

Open questions

  1. Is duckdb worth keeping as a hard Imports for PROC SQL, or should it be a Suggests with a pure-R fallback? It is kept for now.
  2. The vectorised DATA step generator depends on dplyr. Would emitting base R for the common cases (mutate-only steps) be worth the maintenance cost? It would shrink the dependency surface of generated code, not of the engine.
  3. Nothing in the value layer prevents using base R alternatives; the rule is: a tidyverse function may be used where its semantics are exactly the SAS semantics being implemented or do not affect the results, and nowhere else.
